title: Israel and Lebanon agree to implement ceasefire if Hezbollah stops attacks
text:
ADVERTISEMENT
Israel and Lebanon agree to implement ceasefire if Hezbollah stops attacks
4 hours ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
David GrittenandHelen Sullivan
1:50
Watch: Lebanon-Israel ceasefire deal made in 'hope rather than expectation'

Israel and Lebanon have agreed to renew their fragile ceasefire and create a number of "pilot" security zones inside Lebanon in which Hezbollah operatives would be banned, the US state department has announced.

A joint statement said the agreement was "contingent on a complete cessation" of attacks by the Iran-backed armed group Hezbollah, among other conditions.

The three countries also "rejected any attempt, by any state or non-state actor, to hold Lebanon's future hostage".

The agreement was announced in Washington on Wednesday, after Israeli strikes killed at least nine people in southern Lebanon and Hezbollah fired rockets into northern Israel.

Lebanese state media reported that Israeli strikes continued in the south of Lebanon on Thursday, with at least one strike causing casualties.

Hezbollah, a Shia Muslim militia, political party and social movement, is Lebanon's most powerful group. With support from Iran, it has built an armed force more formidable than the Lebanese army and has fought a series of conflicts with Israel. It is designated as a terrorist organisation by Israel and many other countries, including the UK and US.

The agreement between Israel and Lebanon, reached after a fourth round of US-mediated talks, is contingent on the "evacuation of all [Hezbollah] operatives" from an area between the Israeli border and the Litani river, about 30km (19 miles) to the north, which is currently occupied by Israeli ground forces.

It said the US would help guide the creation of "pilot zones in which the Lebanese Armed Forces will take exclusive control of the territory to the exclusion of all non-state actors".

ADVERTISEMENT

It did not include any maps to indicate where the pilot zones would be located, or any explanation of how they might work in practice.

The agreement followed a partial ceasefire announced on Monday, which Lebanon said would see Israel refrain from bombing the Lebanese capital, Beirut, in exchange for Hezbollah not attacking Israel.

The two countries' representatives will meet again on 22 June to hold further talks "with a view toward reaching a comprehensive agreement".

Hezbollah told the BBC that it would comment officially in due course.

Far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir branded the agreement a "serious mistake", claiming it would allow Hezbollah to "grow stronger".

Lebanon was drawn into the war between the US, Israel and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for an Israeli strike that killed Iran's supreme leader. Israel responded with an air campaign across Lebanon and a ground invasion in the south.

A US-brokered ceasefire between Israel and Lebanon on 16 April failed to stop the fighting, and last week Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the Israeli military to intensify its strikes on Hezbollah and advance deeper into Lebanon in response to drone and rocket attacks on communities in northern Israel.

At least 3,516 people have been killed in Lebanon since the start of the war, according to the country's health ministry. Its figures do not distinguish between combatants and civilians.

The UN says more than one million people have also registered themselves as displaced in Lebanon, where Israeli evacuation orders cover more than an eighth of the country.

Israel says 26 of its soldiers and four Israeli civilians have been killed on both sides of the border during the war.

Reuters
Smoke billows from the Nabatieh area in southern Lebanon following an Israeli strike on Wednesday

Lebanese media reported Israeli strikes across the south of the country on Wednesday.

The health ministry said four Syrians and two Palestinians were killed in a strike in the al-Housh area, which is just south of the coastal city of Tyre.

The ministry also said that two paramedics were killed and a third was seriously wounded when Israeli forces "directly targeted an ambulance" in the Chehour area, which is about 14km (9 miles) to the east. The ambulance belonged to the Risala Scouts Association, which is affiliated with the Amal movement, an ally of Hezbollah.

The ministry accused the Israeli military of "demonstrating contempt for international humanitarian law", which specifically protects medical personnel.

At least 128 paramedics and healthcare workers have been killed in Israeli attacks on ambulances and medical facilities over the past three months, according to the ministry.

There was no immediate comment from the Israeli military. In the past, it has claimed that ambulances are being used for military purposes, without providing any evidence.

The Lebanese army, meanwhile, said that one of its soldiers was killed in an Israeli air strike on the road between Nabatieh and Kfar Tebnit, about 27km north-east of Tyre. Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported that his motorbike was targeted by a drone.

The army said another two Lebanese soldiers were injured in a separate Israeli strike on their vehicle on the road between Deir Zahrani and Nabatieh.

It denounced what it called "a pattern of deliberate strikes targeting army personnel, vehicles and positions" by Israeli forces.

NNA also reported an Israeli strike on a car on the busy coastal highway in the Khaldeh area, just south of Beirut. It did not mention any casualties, but security sources told Reuters news agency that two people were injured.

It was the closest strike to the capital since the partial ceasefire was announced.

Reuters
A funeral was held on Wednesday in Wardaniyeh, southern Lebanon, for six members of the same family who were killed in an Israeli strike

Also on Wednesday, the Israeli military said it intercepted a "hostile aircraft" that crossed the border near the Manara and Kiryat Shmona areas, about 15km south of Nabatieh, as well as two projectiles that crossed in the nearby Misgav Am area.

The military did not immediately blame Hezbollah, but the group later said that "in response to the Israeli enemy army's violation of the ceasefire" its fighters targeted "a gathering of Israeli enemy army soldiers" in northern Israel with a rocket barrage.

Israel's leaders have warned that its military would resume strikes on the Hezbollah stronghold of Beirut's southern suburbs, known as Dahieh, if the group launched cross-border attacks on northern Israeli communities.

According to the Lebanese government, the partial ceasefire agreed on Monday states that "Israel will not launch a broad offensive on Beirut in exchange for Hezbollah refraining from launching attacks against Israel".

The government said Hezbollah had confirmed its acceptance, but a member of the group's political council, Mahmoud Qamati, told the BBC on Tuesday: "There was no ceasefire agreement, just the protection of Dahieh."

Qamati also insisted that Hezbollah would not abide by any commitments made at the Lebanese-Israeli talks in Washington.

"We think these negotiations do not concern us, nor do we recognise their findings or decisions, because we have rejected them on principle," he said.

The partial truce was announced by US President Donald Trump, who on Wednesday appeared to confirm a report that it was brokered after he had called Netanyahu "crazy" in an expletive-laden call prompted by the prime minister's order to bomb the Lebanese capital.

Trump is said to be concerned that further escalation in Lebanon could jeopardise a wider deal to end the war between the US, Israel and Iran.

Iran has warned the US that any regional ceasefire must include Lebanon.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Wednesday that if Israeli aggression against Beirut continued, its armed forces were "fully prepared" to resume the war, Iran's Tasnim news agency reported.

title: 10 winning photos from the World Food Photography Awards 2026
text:

10 winning photos from the World Food Photography Awards 2026
1 day ago

Save

BBC Travel
Marco Rutten/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Marco Rutten/ World Food Photography Awards)

From a Soviet-era sanatorium to a floating market in Bangladesh, this year's World Food Photography Awards capture the many ways food shapes daily life around the world.

The 2026 competition, sponsored by Tenderstem® Bimi® Broccolini, drew nearly 9,000 entries from more than 50 countries, immortalising harvests, markets, family kitchens, street food, celebrations and survival. With just one click, food photographers around the world created a global portrait of food culture, showing not just what people eat, but how food is woven into everyday life.

Here are some of this year's most striking winning images.

Jo Kearney/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Jo Kearney/ World Food Photography Awards)
Overall winner: Jo Kearney, UK

British photographer Jo Kearney's winning shot captured a solitary moment in the canteen of a Soviet-era sanatorium in Tajikistan – a reminder that food photography can be as much about evoking memory and place as it is about whetting appetite. At Khoja Obi Garm in the mountains of Tajikistan, guests still gather for simple, hearty meals between prescribed treatments. Built on radon-rich hot springs, the vast concrete "health hotel" once offered workers two weeks of annual rest. Today, its low cost continues to draw local Tajiks, visitors from neighbouring Central Asian countries and the occasional backpacker.

Pingyao Song/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Pingyao Song/ World Food Photography Awards)
Winner, Food for Celebration: Pingyao Song, China

At a hotpot festival in China, hundreds of diners gather around a vast communal banquet. The red broth, rich with chilli, Sichuan peppercorn, fermented bean paste, beef tallow and spices, becomes both meal and spectacle as guests eat, film and livestream the feast.

Albert González/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Albert González/ World Food Photography Awards)
Winner, Cream of the Crop: Albert González, Spain

In Ine, a fishing village in Kyoto Prefecture, Japan, squid dries in the sun using the traditional technique of himono. The preservation method, used for fish and seafood, draws flavour from salt, air and time, linking the village's food traditions to the sea that sustains it.

Marco Rutten/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Marco Rutten/ World Food Photography Awards)
Winner, Bring Home the Harvest: Marco Rutten, Netherlands

At sunrise beneath Kolkata's Howrah Bridge, a small crew hauls in nets from the Hooghly River. Their catch will be sold in nearby markets and cooked that same morning in Bengali homes. The image captures a quiet harvest taking place beneath one of the city's busiest crossings.

Kara Baird/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Kara Baird/ World Food Photography Awards)
Winner, Street Food: Kara Baird, Australia

In Kyoto's Nishiki Market, a fleeting moment is captured through the crush of shoppers, steam, heat and movement. Known as "Kyoto's kitchen", the market has long been one of the city's great food thoroughfares, where street snacks, pickles, seafood and sweets are packed into narrow lanes. This image catches the intensity of the market at its busiest.

Juan Miguel Ortuño Martinez/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Juan Miguel Ortuño Martinez/ World Food Photography Awards)
Winner, Louis Jadot Wine Photographer of the Year: Juan Miguel Ortuño Martinez, Spain

Inside an underground wine tank, a worker cleans away the traces of the previous vintage with pressurised water. After the walls and floor are washed, his partner lowers a small bucket with a sponge inside to collect what remains in the lowest corner. The image reveals the hidden labour behind winemaking that is far from the romance of the glass.

Michela Balboni and Federico Borella/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Michela Balboni and Federico Borella/ World Food Photography Awards)
Winner, Food for the Family: Michela Balboni and Federico Borella, Italy

In Samarkand, Uzbekistan, a child reaches towards hot non bread fresh from the family tandoor. Dense and round with a thick chewy crust, always marked at the centre with black sesame seeds, Samarkand non is one of the city's defining foods.

Indigo Larmour/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Indigo Larmour/ World Food Photography Awards)
Winner, Jamie Oliver Youth Prize 13-17: Indigo Larmour

During Chhath Puja in West Bengal, India, devotees stand in water holding food offerings to Surya, the Sun god. The festival, observed largely by women, is rooted in gratitude, purification and devotion.

Kazi Mohammad Golam Quddus/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Kazi Mohammad Golam Quddus/ World Food Photography Awards)
Winner, Food for Sale: Kazi Mohammad Golam Quddus, Bangladesh

In Bogra, Bangladesh, a vegetable market comes to life in the early morning. Farmers bring their freshly harvested cabbages by rickshaw van before traders buy the produce and send it on to Dhaka and other major cities.

Lehóczki Balázs/ World Food Photography Awards
(Credit: Lehóczki Balázs/ World Food Photography Awards)
Winner, The Philip Harben Award for Food in Action: Lehóczki Balázs

Hungarian photographer Lehóczki Balázs had imagined this portrait of his grandparents for years but felt unworthy of capturing them. His grandmother went to the hairdresser and his grandfather shaved before he set up his studio equipment in their kitchen. When she saw the finished image, his grandmother called him an artist.

The 14-course dinner redefining Zambian cuisine
3 days ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Mazuba Kapambwe
Courtesy of Sungani Restaurant
(Credit: Courtesy of Sungani Restaurant)

Fine dining in Zambia has long meant replicating European techniques. But chef Sungani Phiri's new home restaurant is boldly elevating Zambia's ingredients – and its culinary profile.

I'm sitting at an outdoor verandah with my family in a suburb of Livingstone, Zambia, when chef Sungani Piri brings out our fourth course.

It's a black cone-shaped canape made of cassava, served on a bed of millet inside a black potjie – a three-legged cooking pot. Filled with avocado ice cream and topped with edible gold flecks, it's almost too pretty to eat. But I take a bite; it's simultaneously sweet and savoury. The gold, Phiri informs us, is an homage to the Copperbelt, Zambia's mining region.

These dishes are Zambia on a plate, yet unlike anything most travellers – or locals – will have encountered in the tourist capital, where restaurants usually cater to international tastes and fine dining has long referenced European techniques. Visitors hoping to try traditional Zambian cuisine typically encounter buffets of stews, boiled vegetables and nshima, the porridge-like cornmeal that is our staple food. 

But Sungani Restaurant, whose fine dining tasting menu is entirely rooted in Zambia's indigenous ingredients and culinary memory, offers travellers a whole new way to experience Zambia's flavours – and a window into Zambian culture itself. 

This is also Chef Phiri's home. And there are still 10 courses to go. 

Courtesy of Sungani Restaurant
Phiri's multi-course tasting menu unfolds within his own home (Credit: Courtesy of Sungani Restaurant)
New frontiers

Visitor itineraries to Zambia usually focus on activities that celebrate its immense natural riches, like walking safaris through Mopane forests or hiking the magnificent Victoria Falls; the world's largest waterfall. Rarely do travellers venture to quiet city suburbs, let alone dine there. But just half an hour's drive north of the Falls, Phiri has been quietly developing the country's first molecular gastronomic experience, and making its cuisine a destination in itself. 

Before launching Sungani last year, Phiri trained with two-Michelin-starred chef Sven Niebremer in South Africa, then served as head chef at Royal Chundu lodge in Livingstone and Botanica in Lusaka.

Zambian cuisine deserves to be told on the world stage, on its own terms

Phiri's groundbreaking "New Zambian cuisine" was born from an argument. After culinary school, he planned to embrace the European fine dining techniques he'd been taught. But his sister challenged the notion as "pretentious" if done without grounding them in Zambia itself. Inspired, Phiri decided that his own fine-dining restaurant would elevate Zambia's culinary tradition and began experimenting with ingredients he had grown up eating.

"When I place a chibwantu root in someone's hands before they eat, I'm not just showing them an ingredient – I'm taking them somewhere," he explained. "To the river, to the bush, to a Zambian childhood. For an international guest it opens a door they didn't know existed. For a Zambian guest, it's a moment of recognition and pride – seeing something deeply familiar treated with reverence and wonder."

His decision to host the experience inside his own residence was equally deliberate. "When you want to honour someone here, you don't take them to a restaurant – you bring them to your table," he said.

In April 2025, Phiri welcomed his first guests and launched a tasting menu called The Rebirth. "I’m trying to use food to show the standard of the finest things this country produces and then translate that onto a plate," he said.

Courtesy of Sungani Restaurant
Sungani Restaurant's tasting menu celebrates and elevates Zambia's traditional ingredients (Credit: Courtesy of Sungani Restaurant)
Locally grown, locally loved 

Upon arriving, my family and I are greeted by Alibesi Mwale Phiri, Phiri's wife and director of operations. "Twamilandilani," she said – "welcome" in Nyanja, one of Zambia's many local languages. "Please feel at home."

Plan your trip:

Travellers can reserve a table at Sungani Restaurant via email, phone or the restaurant's website. The tasting menu experience costs $215 USD (£160) and must be paid in advance. Booking at least three days out is recommended, though reservations can be made 7-14 days ahead. Because the menu is driven by seasonality, dishes and the number of courses may vary. 

The restaurant seats just 22 people, with guests dining on a verandah beside the family's open-plan kitchen, divided by an island. A dining table functions both as the "chef's table" and family dining table. Phiri explained that all the restaurant's ingredients are sourced within a 100km radius, with his inspiration coming from farms and fish markets. "What's ready [in season], what's abundant, what's being overlooked. The menu follows that conversation," he said.

Depending on the season, the tasting menu spans 14 to 16 courses, many inspired by the Southern Province, where Livingstone is located. The project also doubles as a training ground for young Zambian chefs, three of whom were waiting on us that evening. "Groups of chefs come to learn here, and the first thing we focus on is indigenous ingredients," Phiri said. "Most young Zambian chefs have never cooked with them seriously."

Fourteen voyages into Zambia 

Dinner begins with a welcome drink made from tart mundambi, Zambian hibiscus, topped with a square of hibiscus candy. The pink, frothy beverage transforms an ingredient more commonly associated with fruit jellies into something elegant and refreshing.

Courtesy of Sungani Restaurant
The ingredients on the tasting menu pay homage to Zambia's provinces (Credit: Courtesy of Sungani Restaurant)

Several starters arrive in slow succession, beginning with a marshmallow made from pureed bondwe, a spinach-like vegetable usually served alongside nshima. The avocado and cassava cone comes next; cold, crunchy and creamy on our tongues. A savoury dumpling filled with free-range "village chicken" is served alongside an egg yolk, julienned carrots and bok choy. We are offered the "onion shot" – shot glasses of room-temperature onion soup – before receiving beef pâté with delele (okra) and crayfish pai tee: crispy pastry shells stuffed with crayfish from the Zambezi River.

Phiri returns with a sheaf of chibwantu reeds in hand for the ninth course, a palate-cleansing cocktail called "Where It All Began". The reeds are used as the raw ingredient in Zambia's traditional fermented beverage, but here it is transformed into a gin-based cocktail served inside a snail shell and garnished with green apple slices.

After a bread and jam platter – called, aptly, "The Journey To Home" – which includes freshly baked cassava wraps and a sweet, dense bread made from mabisi (sour milk), the tasting experience returns to the water. Zambezi bream, a species similar to tilapia, has fed communities along the river for generations and is typically served whole and grilled. Phiri's show-stopping version has thin slices layered into a mosaic and flavoured with lemon zest, ginger syrup and parsley powder. Okra caviar and edible gold flecks complete the dish.

The standout ingredient in the steak course is dried caterpillars (ifinkubala). In traditional Zambian cuisine, they are deep fried, but Phiri grinds them to powder to create the steak rub. "The ingredient is fully present, but the technique creates a bridge," he explained, acknowledging that some international diners may baulk at eating insects.

More like this:

• Chasing the rare lunar 'rainbow' at Victoria Falls

• Zambia is the world's walking safari capital

• Africa's ice cream café that nurtures self-esteem

After the steak, we are ready for something sweet – the final course. We are presented a frozen cube of vitumbuwa cheesecake inspired by the eponymous Zambian-style beignet that is usually eaten as a snack or on-the-go breakfast.  Phiri's version is filled with coffee-flavoured cream, a nod to Zambia's northern coffee-producing region.

"Every region has something to say,"  said Phiri. "The tasting menu is my way of bringing Zambia to one table."

By the time we complete the culinary experience, both our bellies and brains are stuffed with Zambian culinary history. For me and my family, Phiri's dining experience has achieved something simple, yet precious: it showed us how our national cuisine can be elevated, giving us new respect for the beloved ingredients. But most of all, it's putting Zambia on the map, one delicious ingredient at a time.

"Zambian cuisine deserves to be told on the world stage, on its own terms," said Phiri.

OpenHarness is an application that enables AI agents to interact with external tools, manage conversational flows, and automate tasks. It integrates various AI models, including Large Language Models (LLMs), to provide capabilities for tool use, skill application, memory management, and multi-agent coordination.

OpenHarness extends AI agent functionality through several key components:

Plugins (src/openharness/plugins) provide dynamic extensibility, enabling the integration of custom skills, commands, agents, and tools. Plugin Lifecycle and Extensibility details this system.
Skills (src/openharness/skills) encapsulate reusable knowledge and specific functionalities, accessible by AI agents or users as commands. Skill System: Definition, Loading, and Registry provides more information.
Command Management (src/openharness/commands) processes user input and orchestrates application behavior, including interactive commands and skill-based invocations. This is further explained in Centralized Command Management.
Multi-Agent Coordination (src/openharness/coordinator) defines and manages AI agents, their configurations, and their orchestration in team-based scenarios. Refer to Multi-Agent Coordination and Team Orchestration for specifics.
The CLI and Core Application Flow (src/openharness/cli.py) serves as the primary user entry point, supporting interactive sessions, single prompts, and headless operations. See OpenHarness CLI and Core Application Flow.

The system integrates with various AI models through a unified API layer (src/openharness/api), which abstracts interactions with providers such as Anthropic, OpenAI, Codex, and Copilot. This layer manages API calls, streaming responses, error handling, and token usage tracking. Unified AI Model API and Provider Abstraction describes this in more detail. A comprehensive Authentication Management system (src/openharness/auth) handles various authentication flows and securely stores credentials, including integration with external CLI tools. Comprehensive Authentication Management offers further insights.

The Conversation Engine (src/openharness/engine) orchestrates conversational flows. It maintains chat history, manages token usage with auto-compaction, executes tools based on AI model requests, and generates structured stream events for real-time updates. Conversation Engine: History, Token Management, and Tool Execution provides an in-depth look.

OpenHarness also includes distinct agent applications:

ohmo (ohmo) is a personal AI agent that provides a command-line interface, a gateway service for message processing, and manages conversational sessions and personal memory. Ohmo Command-Line Interface and Workspace Management, Ohmo Gateway Service and Message Processing, and Ohmo Session, Memory, and Context Management elaborate on these aspects.
Autopilot (src/openharness/autopilot) automates repository tasks, orchestrating work from intake to execution, including local verification, Git and GitHub integration for pull requests, and policy-driven merges. Autopilot Task Orchestration and Execution and Autopilot Data Models and Reporting explain its mechanics.

User interaction occurs through various interfaces:

A React-based Terminal UI (frontend/terminal) offers an interactive console environment for engaging with AI agents, featuring input handling, conversation display, and a theming system. Details are in React-based Terminal UI: Architecture and Core Components and React-based Terminal UI: Theming System.
A Web Dashboard (autopilot-dashboard) visualizes Autopilot tasks through a kanban board, journal, and pipeline statistics. This is covered in Web Dashboard: Autopilot Visualization and Data Flow and Web Dashboard: Animated SVG Visualizations.

Communication within OpenHarness relies on a message-bus architecture (src/openharness/channels/bus) for decoupled interaction between chat platforms and the AI query engine. Asynchronous Message Bus Core and Channel Abstraction and Lifecycle Management describe how channel lifecycles are managed and messages are routed. The ChannelBridge (src/openharness/channels/adapter.py) facilitates this integration, acting as the intermediary. More information is available in Integration with Query Engine.

Automated Installation Scripts (scripts) streamline the environment setup on various operating systems. Automated Installation Scripts explains the installation process. An End-to-End Testing Framework (.claude and scripts) validates OpenHarness features using real agent loops and LLM API calls, ensuring system integrity. End-to-End Validation and PR Management and End-to-End Testing Framework provide further details.

OpenHarness Architecture and Core Logic
link
zoom_in

OpenHarness provides a foundational framework for developing and operating AI agents, integrating core functionalities like agent orchestration, configuration management, plugin extensibility, and essential utilities. The system is designed to wrap around a Large Language Model (LLM), enabling it to act as a functional agent with capabilities for tool use, skill application, memory management, and multi-agent coordination.

At its core, OpenHarness orchestrates agent interactions through an "Agent Loop" managed by the src/openharness/engine directory. This loop is responsible for querying the LLM API, processing streaming responses, executing tool calls, and determining subsequent actions based on tool results. Key considerations in this loop include permission checks and the integration of event-driven hooks.

The application's settings and operational parameters are managed through a multi-layer configuration system, primarily defined within the src/openharness/config directory. This system handles the loading and persistence of settings, including provider profiles for various AI models, API keys, and communication channel configurations. It uses Pydantic models for schema validation, ensuring consistency and structured data handling. Configuration paths are resolved consistently across platforms, adhering to XDG-like conventions. For further details on how OpenHarness handles its configurations, see OpenHarness CLI and Core Application Flow and Comprehensive Authentication Management.

Extensibility is a central tenet of OpenHarness, largely facilitated by its plugin system located in the src/openharness/plugins directory. This system manages the lifecycle of plugins, from discovery and loading to installation and uninstallation. Plugins are structured via manifest files that define their components, such as custom skills, commands, agents, tools, hooks, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) configurations, allowing developers to extend the application's capabilities dynamically. Additional information on plugins can be found in Plugin Lifecycle and Extensibility.

Similarly, skills—which represent on-demand knowledge or specific functionalities—are managed within the src/openharness/skills directory. The system defines SkillDefinition objects, manages the loading of skills from various sources (including bundled and user-defined Markdown files), and maintains a SkillRegistry for efficient storage and retrieval. YAML frontmatter in Markdown files is used to extract metadata for these skills. For more about skills, see Skill System: Definition, Loading, and Registry.

Command management, particularly for interactive operations within the application, is centralized in the src/openharness/commands directory. The CommandRegistry is responsible for defining, registering, and executing commands. It provides a CommandContext to handlers, ensuring they have the necessary operational context, and standardizes return values through CommandResult to control application flow. Refer to Centralized Command Management for more information.

For multi-agent scenarios, the src/openharness/coordinator directory provides the framework for defining and orchestrating AI agents. It handles AgentDefinition configurations, manages teams through a TeamRegistry, and generates coordinator prompts for inter-agent communication and task notifications. This enables complex team-based operations and subagent spawning. More details on multi-agent capabilities are available in Multi-Agent Coordination and Team Orchestration.

The integrity and reliability of OpenHarness features are ensured through rigorous end-to-end validation processes. The .claude directory, particularly within .claude/skills/harness-eval, contains a testing framework that uses real agent loops and LLM API calls on unfamiliar codebases, rather than relying on mocks. This validation approach is crucial for verifying the system's behavior in realistic operational environments. Additionally, the .claude/skills/pr-merge subdirectory outlines a contributor-first approach to managing external pull requests, focusing on preserving author attribution, resolving conflicts post-merge, and allowing selective merges, which reflects a robust approach to community contributions. See End-to-End Validation and PR Management for more details.

OpenHarness CLI and Core Application Flow
link
zoom_in

The OpenHarness command-line interface (CLI) acts as the primary entry point for users to interact with the system, orchestrating agent execution, configuration management, and various operational modes. The main executable for the openharness package is located at src/openharness/__main__.py, which invokes the app object defined in src/openharness/cli.py.

The core typer application, app, in src/openharness/cli.py is responsible for handling user input and dispatching commands. It supports several operational modes:

REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop): An interactive session for continuous interaction with AI agents.
Single-prompt execution: For executing a specific command or prompt without entering an interactive session.
Headless task worker: For running background tasks without direct user interaction.

A key feature of the CLI is its --dry-run mode, which allows users to preview the resolved runtime configuration and capabilities of OpenHarness without actual execution. This dry-run preview details how the system would interpret a command, what resources it would utilize, and provides insights into system readiness and potential issues. This functionality is supported by internal functions such as _build_dry_run_preview, _format_dry_run_preview, and _evaluate_dry_run_readiness in src/openharness/cli.py.

The CLI also integrates various sub-applications to manage specific features through typer.Typer instances. These sub-applications, including mcp_app, plugin_app, auth_app, provider_app, cron_app, and autopilot_app, provide specialized command sets for managing Micro-Controller Protocol (MCP) servers, plugins, authentication, AI provider profiles, scheduled tasks, and the autopilot system, respectively. This modular structure enhances maintainability and user discoverability of commands.

For interactive configuration, the setup_cmd in src/openharness/cli.py provides a guided flow for setting up provider profiles and authenticating with AI providers. Similarly, auth_login offers an interactive command for managing login and binding processes for various AI services.

The system relies on openharness.config.load_settings and save_settings for persistent management of user and session configurations. Session management is also supported, allowing users to continue or resume previous sessions by ID, facilitating workflow continuity.

The CLI's design prioritizes user experience with interactive prompts, ensuring intuitive terminal interactions for configuration and authentication processes, while falling back to simpler prompts if advanced capabilities are unavailable. Further details on configuration management can be found in OpenHarness Architecture and Core Logic.

Centralized Command Management
link
zoom_in

The OpenHarness application features a robust command management system that orchestrates user interactions, application state modifications, and integration with various functionalities. This system is primarily managed through the CommandRegistry and relies on CommandContext to provide handlers with necessary information and CommandResult to standardize their outcomes.

The CommandRegistry is a central component defined in src/openharness/commands/registry.py. It is responsible for storing and retrieving commands, enabling both direct command execution and dynamic integration of skill-based commands. This registry allows for the registration of SlashCommand objects, which encapsulate the command's name, description, handler function, and aliases. When a user input is received, the CommandRegistry can parse it to identify the command and its arguments, facilitating its execution.

Command handlers, which are asynchronous functions, receive a CommandContext object. This object provides a comprehensive set of dependencies and contextual information required for command execution, such as the QueryEngine for AI model interaction, the current working directory, tool registries, application state, and session-related information. This approach ensures that command handlers operate with all necessary data without needing to access global state directly, promoting modularity and testability.

Upon execution, command handlers return a CommandResult object. This standardized return value, also defined in src/openharness/commands/registry.py, dictates how the application should behave after a command is processed. It can include a message to display to the user, instructions to exit the application, clear the screen, replay messages, or control the continuation of pending operations or turns. This mechanism provides a clear and consistent way for commands to influence the overall application flow.

The system supports a wide array of built-in commands for managing application settings, session history, project development tools, and diagnostic information. Furthermore, OpenHarness's skill system allows for dynamic registration of skills as slash commands, extending the application's capabilities based on loaded plugins. This integration is facilitated by functions like lookup_skill_slash_command and _register_user_invocable_skill_commands in src/openharness/commands/registry.py, ensuring that user-defined skills can seamlessly become part of the interactive command set. For more details on skills, see Skill System: Definition, Loading, and Registry.

The public interface for the command package, defined in src/openharness/commands/__init__.py, exposes these core components, making them readily available for use throughout the OpenHarness codebase. This structure ensures that the command management system is both powerful and easy to integrate for new features and extensions.

Plugin Lifecycle and Extensibility
link
zoom_in

OpenHarness incorporates a plugin system designed for extensibility, allowing for the dynamic integration of custom functionalities such as skills, commands, agents, tools, hooks, and MCP (Multi-Configuration Project) configurations. This system manages the complete lifecycle of plugins, from discovery and loading to installation and uninstallation, all structured around well-defined manifests.

The core of plugin management is initiated through src/openharness/plugins/__init__.py, which provides deferred imports for essential functions. These include discover_plugin_paths to locate available plugins, load_plugins to integrate them into the application, and install_plugin_from_path and uninstall_plugin for managing user-specific plugins. This approach ensures that modules are only loaded when their symbols are accessed, optimizing startup performance.

Plugins are defined by a PluginManifest, a Pydantic model specified in src/openharness/plugins/schemas.py. This manifest dictates the structure and validation rules for plugin metadata, including its name, version, description, and whether it is enabled_by_default. It also specifies paths to various plugin components, such as skills_dir, tools_dir, hooks_file, and mcp_file, ensuring consistency across all plugin configurations.

The discovery and loading of plugins are orchestrated by src/openharness/plugins/loader.py. This module identifies plugin directories by searching for plugin.json manifests and then parses each plugin's components. It employs functions to load skills, commands, agent definitions, event hooks, MCP server configurations, and tools. Notably, src/openharness/plugins/loader.py can dynamically import and instantiate tool classes from Python files, providing a flexible mechanism for extending the system with custom functionalities without requiring explicit registration. Skills, commands, and agents often use YAML frontmatter within Markdown files for metadata, allowing for rich configuration directly within content files. The system allows for project-local plugins, with warnings if they are disabled, to mitigate risks from untrusted workspaces.

For managing user-installed plugins, src/openharness/plugins/installer.py provides utilities for installation and uninstallation. This module ensures that plugin names are valid and prevents path traversal vulnerabilities, safeguarding the integrity of the user's plugin directory. It can install a plugin by copying its contents from a source path and uninstall it by removing its directory. The _resolve_user_plugin_dir function is central to validating plugin names and paths, contributing to the security of the installation process.

Once loaded, plugins are represented at runtime by the LoadedPlugin dataclass, defined in src/openharness/plugins/types.py. This dataclass encapsulates the plugin's manifest, its file system path, and its enabled status, along with lists of its contributed skills, commands, agents, and tools, and dictionaries for hooks and mcp_servers. Similarly, individual plugin commands are represented by the PluginCommandDefinition dataclass, holding details like name, description, and content. These data structures facilitate the dynamic integration and management of plugin functionalities within OpenHarness. The src/openharness/plugins/bundled directory currently serves as a placeholder, with no bundled plugins implemented.

Skill System: Definition, Loading, and Registry
link
zoom_in

OpenHarness incorporates a skill system for defining, loading, and managing encapsulated functionalities, ranging from developer best practices to specific operational tasks. This system enables the application to dynamically extend its capabilities and adapt to user needs.

At the core of the skill system is the SkillDefinition data model, defined in src/openharness/skills/types.py. This immutable data structure captures essential metadata for each skill, including its unique name, a description of its purpose, the actual skill content (often in Markdown), its origin (source), and various optional attributes like a command_name for CLI invocation, a display_name, aliases, and flags indicating whether it is user_invocable or if disable_model_invocation applies. This comprehensive definition allows the system to understand and categorize skills effectively.

Skills are discovered and loaded from multiple sources, providing flexibility and extensibility. The load_skill_registry function, located in src/openharness/skills/loader.py, orchestrates this process. It first incorporates "bundled" skills, which are predefined functionalities shipped with OpenHarness. These bundled skills, found in src/openharness/skills/bundled/content, often document development best practices such as creating Git commits, debugging, planning, or reviewing code. They serve as foundational capabilities and examples for skill design. Beyond bundled skills, the system also loads user-defined skills from a designated user configuration directory (retrieved via get_user_skills_dir) and can integrate skills embedded within installed plugins. Skill discovery typically involves scanning directories for SKILL.md files, parsing their content, and extracting metadata and frontmatter using utilities from src/openharness/skills/_frontmatter.py. These parsing functions are responsible for interpreting YAML frontmatter to populate the SkillDefinition attributes, ensuring consistent handling of skill metadata.

Once skills are discovered and parsed into SkillDefinition objects, they are registered within a SkillRegistry, implemented in src/openharness/skills/registry.py. This registry acts as a central repository, allowing skills to be looked up by their name, command name, display name, or any defined aliases. This flexible retrieval mechanism ensures that the application can efficiently access and invoke skills based on various user inputs or internal triggers. The SkillRegistry also provides functionality to list all unique registered skills, de-duplicating entries and sorting them for coherent presentation. The src/openharness/skills/__init__.py file acts as the package's facade, providing unified access to these core skill-related components through lazy loading, which helps optimize startup performance by only importing modules when their contents are actually needed.

Multi-Agent Coordination and Team Orchestration
link
zoom_in

The OpenHarness multi-agent system uses a framework for defining and managing AI agents and their coordination. This includes configurations for individual agents, a registry for managing teams, and mechanisms for generating coordinator prompts and handling inter-agent communication and task notifications.

Agent definitions are managed by the AgentDefinition Pydantic BaseModel defined in src/openharness/coordinator/agent_definitions.py. This model encapsulates an agent's configurable fields, such as its name, description, system_prompt, tools, model, effort, permission_mode, max_turns, skills, mcp_servers, hooks, color, background, initial_prompt, memory, and isolation. The system pre-configures a set of built-in agents, each with specific system prompts and tool access tailored to their roles. Agent definitions can also be loaded from user-defined directories and dynamically from enabled plugins, with newer definitions overriding older ones based on the source. Functions such as has_required_mcp_servers and filter_agents_by_mcp_requirements allow agents to be selected based on the availability of required MCP (Multi-Cloud Platform) servers.

Team management is handled by the TeamRegistry class in src/openharness/coordinator/coordinator_mode.py. This registry allows for the creation, deletion, and management of TeamRecord objects, which track teams by name, description, associated agents (by task ID), and messages. The registry facilitates adding agents to teams and sending messages within a team context.

For inter-agent communication, TaskNotification is a dataclass representing a structured result from a completed agent task. This includes the task_id, status, summary, and optional result and usage information. These notifications can be serialized to and deserialized from XML strings using helper functions such as format_task_notification and parse_task_notification, ensuring structured communication of task outcomes.

The system also defines and manages coordinator-specific behaviors and prompts. The is_coordinator_mode function checks an environment variable to determine if the process is running in coordinator mode. The get_coordinator_system_prompt function dynamically generates a detailed system prompt for the coordinator, outlining its role, available tools (such as agent, send_message, and task_stop), worker management instructions (spawning, continuing, stopping), task workflow, concurrency guidelines, verification procedures, and failure handling. This prompt adapts based on environment variables like CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE to adjust the complexity of worker capabilities presented to the coordinator. The get_coordinator_user_context function provides the coordinator with a workerToolsContext that details the tools available to workers, further informing the coordinator's decision-making process.

End-to-End Validation and PR Management
link
zoom_in

End-to-end validation of OpenHarness features is achieved through real agent loops and LLM API calls on unfamiliar codebases, ensuring that the full system stack operates as intended in realistic scenarios. This process focuses on confirming correct interaction between the API client, model, tool calls, execution, and result processing. Key principles include testing on unfamiliar projects to prevent agents from modifying their own code, using actual API calls rather than mocks, and verifying multi-turn conversations for context reuse. Validation also integrates features like hooks, skills, and agent loop components, with an emphasis on inspecting tool call lists and output files to verify successful tool execution. This approach is detailed in .claude/skills/harness-eval/SKILL.md and supported by a comprehensive feature test matrix in .claude/skills/harness-eval/references/feature-matrix.md.

For managing external pull requests, OpenHarness adopts a contributor-first approach, prioritizing the preservation of author attribution. This methodology emphasizes merging a pull request first and resolving any conflicts afterward, rather than rewriting a contributor's work. The process allows for selective merging, where specific files or features can be excluded from a merge if already implemented locally, provided such exclusions are documented. It explicitly advises against using git apply followed by a self-commit, as this can lead to the loss of original author attribution. The workflow involves triaging pull requests, merging straightforward ones via GitHub's gh pr merge --squash command, and handling more complex scenarios, such as local conflicts or selective merges, using git fetch, git merge, git apply, and git commit with explicit author attribution. Detailed examples for various merge scenarios and command-line instructions are provided in .claude/skills/pr-merge/references/merge-scenarios.md. A pull request template within .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md guides contributors in documenting problem descriptions, changes, and mandatory validation steps, including linting and backend tests. This ensures code quality and provides a structured approach for maintaining project integrity while respecting contributor efforts.

AI Model Integration and Conversation Engine
link
zoom_in

OpenHarness integrates various AI model providers, manages API calls and authentication, and orchestrates conversational flows. The system provides a unified API for interacting with AI models, a conversation engine that manages chat history and token usage, and mechanisms for tool execution and contextual memory.

The system's core API layer, found in src/openharness/api, unifies interactions with multiple AI model providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible APIs, Codex, and Copilot. This layer handles API calls, streams responses, manages authentication, and processes errors with retry logic. It also tracks token usage and dynamically detects provider capabilities based on settings and a centralized registry of LLM provider metadata. For example, AnthropicApiClient in src/openharness/api/client.py and OpenAICompatibleClient in src/openharness/api/openai_client.py are responsible for specific provider interactions, while _is_retryable in src/openharness/api/client.py and _translate_error in src/openharness/api/openai_client.py manage error handling and retries. The ProviderInfo dataclass in src/openharness/api/provider.py provides metadata for the active provider, including authentication type and voice support. A central registry, defined in src/openharness/api/registry.py, holds metadata for various LLM providers and enables auto-detection based on API keys, base URLs, or model names. Token usage is tracked using the UsageSnapshot model in src/openharness/api/usage.py.

A comprehensive authentication system, located in src/openharness/auth, manages authentication states, provider profiles, and credential interactions. This includes handling various authentication flows such as API Key, Device Code, and Browser-based authentication, as described in src/openharness/auth/flows.py. Secure credential storage is managed with fallback mechanisms, prioritizing the system's keyring and falling back to a JSON file if needed, as outlined in src/openharness/auth/storage.py. The AuthManager in src/openharness/auth/manager.py serves as the central interface for managing authentication states and profiles. Integration with external CLI-managed credentials for providers like Codex and Claude is handled by src/openharness/auth/external.py, which includes mechanisms for loading, refreshing, and describing the state of these external bindings. For instance, refresh_claude_oauth_credential in src/openharness/auth/external.py specifically manages the OAuth token refresh for Claude credentials. GitHub Copilot authentication is handled by copilot_api_base and save_copilot_auth in src/openharness/api/copilot_auth.py, managing device-flow authentication and persisting tokens. Custom exception types such as AuthenticationFailure and RateLimitFailure in src/openharness/api/errors.py provide structured error reporting for API interactions.

The QueryEngine, found in src/openharness/engine, is responsible for orchestrating the conversational flow. It manages conversation history, dynamically compacts messages to respect token usage limits (e.g., auto_compact_if_needed in src/openharness/engine/query.py), and executes tools based on AI model requests. The run_query asynchronous generator in src/openharness/engine/query.py handles the iterative process of calling the language model, processing responses, and executing tools, yielding StreamEvent objects for real-time updates. Data models for messages, such as ConversationMessage, TextBlock, ImageBlock, ToolUseBlock, and ToolResultBlock, are defined in src/openharness/engine/messages.py, providing a structured way to represent various content types. The sanitize_conversation_messages function in src/openharness/engine/messages.py ensures conversation history is prepared correctly for AI providers by removing malformed turns. The CostTracker in src/openharness/engine/cost_tracker.py aggregates token usage metrics throughout a session. The QueryEngine also maintains contextual memory, tracking agent goals, invoked skills, and work logs in tool_metadata within the QueryContext (defined in src/openharness/engine/query.py), enabling persistence across turns.

Unified AI Model API and Provider Abstraction
link
zoom_in

The core API layer of OpenHarness provides a unified interface for interacting with various AI model providers, such as Anthropic, Codex, Copilot, and OpenAI-compatible services. This abstraction manages common API concerns including making API calls, streaming responses, handling errors with built-in retry logic, and tracking token usage. The system dynamically detects provider capabilities based on user settings and a central registry of Large Language Model (LLM) provider metadata.

At its foundation, the system uses client classes like AnthropicApiClient in src/openharness/api/client.py, CodexApiClient in src/openharness/api/codex_client.py, and OpenAICompatibleClient in src/openharness/api/openai_client.py to standardize interactions across different AI providers. The CopilotClient in src/openharness/api/copilot_client.py leverages OpenAICompatibleClient while adding Copilot-specific authentication and header requirements. These clients are designed to translate internal OpenHarness message and tool formats into the specific structures required by each provider's API. This ensures that the core application logic can interact with diverse models without needing to implement provider-specific code for each one.

A critical aspect of this API layer is its robust error handling and retry mechanisms. When an API call encounters a transient issue, the system employs exponential backoff with jitter to retry the request. Specific error conditions, such as authentication failures or rate limiting, are translated into a hierarchy of custom exceptions, including AuthenticationFailure and RateLimitFailure, all inheriting from OpenHarnessApiError as defined in src/openharness/api/errors.py. This provides a consistent and actionable error reporting mechanism for the application.

Authentication is managed comprehensively, including specific logic for GitHub Copilot OAuth device-flow authentication detailed in src/openharness/api/copilot_auth.py. This module handles device code requests, polling for access tokens, and securely persists authentication information. For other providers, authentication details are resolved via settings, ensuring credentials are handled appropriately across the system.

The system also includes mechanisms for dynamically inferring provider capabilities and authentication status. The detect_provider function in src/openharness/api/provider.py identifies the active LLM provider, its authentication method, and whether it supports advanced features like voice interactions or multimodal input. This detection leverages a central PROVIDERS registry, defined in src/openharness/api/registry.py, which stores metadata for various LLM providers, including keywords for auto-detection based on model names, API key prefixes, or base URLs. This registry ensures consistent identification and configuration of providers.

Finally, token usage is tracked consistently across all providers using the UsageSnapshot data model from src/openharness/api/usage.py. This model captures input and output token counts, allowing for cost estimation and monitoring of API interactions. These core API components are exposed via src/openharness/api/__init__.py, serving as the primary interface for the rest of the OpenHarness application.

Comprehensive Authentication Management
link
zoom_in

OpenHarness features a centralized authentication system designed to manage user authentication across various providers and credential types. The system provides flexible mechanisms for storing, retrieving, and managing credentials, including integration with external command-line interface (CLI) managed credentials.

The core of this system is the AuthManager class, located in src/openharness/auth/manager.py, which acts as the primary interface for managing authentication states, provider profiles, and interactions with credentials. It handles operations such as retrieving active provider and profile names, listing and managing profiles (creating, updating, removing), and determining authentication statuses for various sources. The AuthManager integrates with OpenHarness settings for configuration and persistence, ensuring that authentication preferences are maintained across sessions.

OpenHarness supports several authentication flows to accommodate different provider requirements:

API Key Flow: Handled by ApiKeyFlow in src/openharness/auth/flows.py, this flow directly prompts the user for an API key.
Device Code Flow: Implemented by DeviceCodeFlow in src/openharness/auth/flows.py, this flow orchestrates the GitHub OAuth device-code process. It guides the user through device code submission and then polls for the access token. This flow is general enough to be used with any GitHub OAuth application that supports device codes. For more details on the unified AI model API, see Unified AI Model API and Provider Abstraction.
Browser Flow: The BrowserFlow in src/openharness/auth/flows.py opens a specified URL in a web browser for user authentication and then prompts the user to paste the obtained token or code back into the terminal.

For credential storage, OpenHarness offers a robust system with a secure fallback mechanism described in src/openharness/auth/storage.py. It prioritizes the use of the system keyring for sensitive secrets. If keyring is unavailable or explicitly disabled, the system falls back to a file-based JSON store, which is located at ~/.openharness/credentials.json. This file-based storage is protected by restricted file permissions (mode 0o600) and uses file locking and atomic writes to ensure data integrity and prevent race conditions. The module also includes non-cryptographic obfuscation functions for non-sensitive data, clearly marked as unsuitable for secure encryption.

The system also integrates with external CLI-managed credentials for specific AI providers, such as Codex and Claude. The src/openharness/auth/external.py module manages the loading, refreshing, and description of these external credentials. It handles different storage mechanisms, including JSON files and the macOS Keychain, and implements OAuth 2.0 refresh token flows for providers like Claude to ensure continuous authentication without requiring repeated manual intervention. This external integration allows OpenHarness to leverage existing authentication setups managed by other tools, streamlining the user experience for developers who might already have credentials configured through CLI applications.

Conversation Engine: History, Token Management, and Tool Execution
link
zoom_in

The QueryEngine within src/openharness/engine is central to managing the conversational flow with AI agents. It orchestrates the process from user input to AI response, integrating various components for robust and dynamic interaction. This engine maintains the conversation history, dynamically manages token usage, facilitates iterative AI model calls, executes tools with permission checks, and generates structured stream events for real-time updates to connected clients.

The QueryEngine is initialized with an api_client for AI model interaction, a tool_registry for managing available tools, and a permission_checker to enforce access controls. It also supports configurable parameters such as the AI model, system_prompt, max_tokens, context_window_tokens, and max_turns, allowing for flexible adaptation to different conversational scenarios.

The conversation history is maintained as a list of ConversationMessage objects, representing various content types including text, images, tool usage, and tool results, defined in src/openharness/engine/messages.py. The engine supports clearing the conversation history or loading new message sequences. A crucial aspect of history management is _build_coordinator_context_message, which can inject context from a coordinator to enrich the AI's understanding.

When a user submits a message, the QueryEngine initiates a query loop. This loop, primarily managed by the run_query function in src/openharness/engine/query.py, iteratively calls the language model, processes its responses, and executes any requested tools. To manage computational resources and ensure efficient interaction, the engine employs a dynamic token usage management strategy, including auto-compaction of the conversation history when token limits are approached. This process yields CompactProgressEvents, providing transparency into how the conversation is being condensed.

Tool execution is a key feature, allowing the AI agent to interact with external systems. When the model requests tool use, the _execute_tool_call function in src/openharness/engine/query.py validates the request, performs necessary permission checks via the permission_checker, executes the tool, and formats its output. The system also handles large tool outputs by offloading them to files, preventing them from saturating the conversational context. The engine maintains a contextual memory through the tool_metadata dictionary, tracking agent activities such as goals, read files, invoked skills, and verified work. This structured memory informs subsequent model prompts and reasoning processes.

The QueryEngine handles potential API errors, such as those related to token limits, by attempting reactive compaction or adjusting max_tokens before retrying. Errors, status updates, and progress information are communicated through structured StreamEvent objects, defined in src/openharness/engine/stream_events.py. These events, such as AssistantTextDelta for incremental responses and AssistantTurnComplete for turn finalization, enable clients to provide real-time feedback and updates to the user. The CostTracker in src/openharness/engine/cost_tracker.py aggregates usage metrics like input and output tokens across the session.

Agent Applications: ohmo and Autopilot
link
zoom_in

ohmo is a personal AI agent application built on OpenHarness, designed to assist users with various tasks. It provides a command-line interface, a core gateway service for message processing, and mechanisms for managing conversational sessions and personal memory.

The ohmo application's primary entry point is through its command-line interface, handled by ohmo/__main__.py, which in turn invokes the app function from ohmo/cli.py. This CLI allows users to launch ohmo in different operational modes, including an interactive terminal UI, a print-only mode for single prompts, or a backend-only mode for service-oriented deployments. It also provides commands for workspace initialization, configuration of AI provider profiles and communication channels, and management of personal memory entries.

The core of ohmo's messaging and AI processing capabilities is the OhmoGatewayService, defined in ohmo/gateway/service.py. This service manages its own lifecycle (start, stop, restart) and state persistence. The OhmoGatewayBridge, located at ohmo/gateway/bridge.py, acts as an intermediary, consuming messages from a message bus, routing them to the appropriate session-aware AI runtime, and publishing replies back to the bus. It also handles special commands (e.g., /stop, /restart) and applies policies for processing messages from group chats, such as those on Feishu, to ensure that ohmo responds appropriately based on mentions or group management status. The OhmoSessionRuntimePool in ohmo/gateway/runtime.py manages independent AI runtime environments for each chat session, ensuring conversations are isolated and stateful. This pool handles the actual interaction with the AI model, persists conversation snapshots, and integrates with specific tools like OhmoCreateFeishuGroupTool in ohmo/gateway/group_tool.py for dynamic group creation. Configuration for the gateway is managed through ohmo/gateway/config.py using Pydantic models like GatewayConfig from ohmo/gateway/models.py, which define settings such as enabled channels, provider profiles, and behavior flags.

ohmo maintains persistent conversational state through a session management system. The module ohmo/session_storage.py is responsible for saving and loading session snapshots, including conversation messages, AI model usage data, and other metadata. This allows ohmo to resume conversations across restarts and provides a history for review. Personal memory entries are managed by the ohmo/memory.py module, which stores them as Markdown files and maintains an index file. Users can list, add, and remove these memory entries, which ohmo can then incorporate into its understanding and responses. Prompts, such as system prompts for the AI model, are dynamically assembled by ohmo/prompts.py. This module combines various contextual elements like the ohmo's "soul" and user profile, workspace details, and personal memory entries to create a comprehensive prompt that guides the AI's behavior. The ohmo workspace structure itself, including the organization of directories for memories, skills, plugins, and sessions, is managed by ohmo/workspace.py.

In addition to ohmo, the system includes an Autopilot feature for managing project-level tasks and automation within a repository. The core of this system is the RepoAutopilotStore, defined in src/openharness/autopilot/service.py. This class orchestrates the lifecycle of automated tasks, represented by RepoTaskCard objects, which are defined along with other data models in src/openharness/autopilot/types.py. The Autopilot manages task intake from various sources (e.g., GitHub issues, internal requests), prioritizes them, and executes them using language models. During execution, it can perform actions like generating code, running local verification steps (e.g., tests), committing changes to Git, creating or updating GitHub Pull Requests, and monitoring CI/CD statuses. The Autopilot includes a repair loop, allowing it to attempt to fix issues encountered during execution and verification by re-engaging the language model with failure context. It maintains a chronological journal of activities and generates an active_context summary to provide an overview of its ongoing work. The Autopilot can also generate dashboards for comprehensive reporting of its operations and outcomes.

Ohmo Command-Line Interface and Workspace Management
link
zoom_in

The ohmo command-line interface, defined primarily in ohmo/cli.py, serves as the primary user interaction point for the personal AI agent. It allows users to launch the agent in various operational modes and manage its workspace, configuration, and personal memory. The application's main entry point is through ohmo/__main__.py, which invokes the CLI.

Users can operate ohmo in different modes:

Interactive TUI (Terminal User Interface): This is the default interactive experience, providing a rich, React-based interface for conversation with the AI agent. The launch_ohmo_react_tui function in ohmo/runtime.py is responsible for setting up and launching this UI, including managing frontend dependencies and embedding the backend command.
Print Mode: For single-prompt execution where the agent processes input and prints the output directly to the console. This mode, handled by run_ohmo_print_mode in ohmo/runtime.py, is useful for scripting or quick, non-interactive queries.
Backend-Only Mode: This mode runs the ohmo agent's core processing logic without a user interface, often used when the agent is integrated into other systems or for specific background tasks. The run_ohmo_backend function in ohmo/runtime.py configures and runs this core host. Users can also resume previous sessions by ID or continue the latest session.

The CLI provides extensive commands for workspace management. The init_cmd subcommand (within ohmo/cli.py) handles the initialization of the ohmo workspace, setting up the necessary directory structure and populating it with template files for the agent's "soul," user profile, and memory. This ensures a consistent and ready-to-use environment. The ohmo/workspace.py module contains core functions like get_workspace_root, ensure_workspace, and initialize_workspace that define and maintain this structure. For diagnostics, the doctor_cmd command leverages workspace_health (also in ohmo/workspace.py) to report on the status and readiness of workspace assets and configured AI providers.

Configuration utilities are also central to the ohmo CLI. The config_cmd (in ohmo/cli.py) provides an interactive wizard (_run_gateway_config_wizard) for setting up provider profiles and communication channels for the ohmo gateway. This includes configuring which AI model providers to use and enabling specific message channels (e.g., Feishu, Slack). The GatewayConfig model defined in ohmo/gateway/models.py structures these settings, and load_gateway_config and save_gateway_config (in ohmo/gateway/config.py) manage their persistence. Additionally, the gateway subcommand provides controls for the OhmoGatewayService (defined in ohmo/gateway/service.py), allowing users to start, stop, restart, and check the status of the background gateway process. This gateway is responsible for bridging message bus channels to the AI processing engine, as detailed in Ohmo Gateway Service and Message Processing. Commands related to provider and model configuration for the gateway are managed by handle_gateway_provider_command and handle_gateway_model_command located in ohmo/gateway/provider_commands.py.

Ohmo Gateway Service and Message Processing
link
zoom_in

The ohmo gateway service bridges message bus channels with the AI processing engine, facilitating multi-session, multi-user interactions. The service manages its own lifecycle, from starting and stopping to restarting, and maintains its operational state.

The core of this service is the OhmoGatewayService class, defined in ohmo/gateway/service.py. This class orchestrates the initialization of various components such as the MessageBus, ChannelManager, and OhmoSessionRuntimePool. It handles the service's startup by writing its process ID to a file and updating its runtime state, and ensures graceful shutdown by setting up signal handlers and cleaning up state files. A key feature of the OhmoGatewayService is its restart mechanism. A request_restart function can initiate a restart, allowing the service to update its configuration or code without manual intervention. The service also manages group creation, particularly for platforms like Feishu, allowing the AI to facilitate setting up managed chat groups and sending welcome messages.

Core Platform Architecture and Development
link

The OpenClaw platform is a local-first AI assistant designed for multi-channel interaction, voice control, and a customizable tool ecosystem. Its core architecture emphasizes a lean kernel with extensive plugin capabilities, enabling a flexible and extensible system. The Gateway serves as the central control plane, orchestrating sessions, channels, tools, and events across the platform. The project vision outlines these principles, with plugins categorized into "Code plugins" and "Bundle-style plugins" Core Platform Vision and Architectural Principles. Security is a paramount concern, addressed through an operator trust model, trusted plugins, and internal security scanning processes, with guidelines for vulnerability reporting Security Considerations and Policies.

The platform's functionality is enabled by foundational SDKs and shared Swift packages. The OpenClawKit provides core utilities, while OpenClawProtocol defines the communication models for interacting with the gateway, such as ConnectParams, RequestFrame, and ResponseFrame. These components facilitate robust and standardized communication within the OpenClaw ecosystem, particularly for features like chat interface components provided by OpenClawChatUI Shared SDKs and Protocols.

Application development for OpenClaw spans multiple platforms, ensuring a broad reach and diverse interaction methods. For mobile and desktop users, client applications are available on Android, iOS, and macOS. The Android application focuses on gateway interaction, device integrations (e.g., camera, location, contacts), and voice control. The iOS application acts as a node, exposing device capabilities to the Gateway, managing connections, and integrating services like push notifications and widgets. The macOS application and its Command-Line Interface (CLI) handle inter-process communication, gateway discovery, and provide menu bar application functionality. These platform-specific implementations leverage frameworks such as Jetpack Compose for Android and OpenClawChatUI for SwiftUI components on iOS Cross-Platform Application Development.

Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) workflows and stringent development standards are central to OpenClaw's development lifecycle. The project leverages automated agents for documentation and testing, defines Docker images for consistent environments, and maintains comprehensive guidelines for tech stack choices, code quality, and contribution processes CI/CD Workflows and Development Standards. Automated agent skills, ranging from code review and release management to testing and data archiving, further streamline development and maintenance efforts Automated Agent Skills and Maintainer Notes.

Core Platform Vision and Architectural Principles
link

The OpenClaw platform is designed as a local-first AI assistant, enabling multi-channel interaction, voice control, and a customizable tool ecosystem. Its core vision, articulated in the project's root README.md, emphasizes operating on local devices while supporting interaction with remote infrastructure. Agent Client Protocol (ACP) and Runtime Architecture
link

The Agent Client Protocol (ACP) system provides the foundational infrastructure for managing and executing AI agent processes within OpenClaw. It establishes a secure and observable environment for agent operations, encompassing client-side integration, session management, policy enforcement, event logging, and a robust runtime for process execution.

A core aspect of the ACP is its client-side implementation, which manages interactions between external clients and the ACP server. This includes resolving tool invocation commands, preparing the execution environment by stripping sensitive information like provider authentication environment variables, and handling user prompts for permission requests. The system classifies tool calls based on their nature (e.g., read-only, execution-capable, mutating) to determine if they can be automatically approved or require explicit user interaction, thereby balancing security with user experience. Utilities in src/acp/client-helpers.ts and the main client in src/acp/client.ts facilitate these operations.

The ACP control plane is responsible for the lifecycle management of agent sessions. A dedicated AcpSessionManager handles the initialization, execution, and termination of sessions, ensuring consistent state and efficient resource use. This includes identity reconciliation for session consistency and dynamic application of runtime controls. This manager, primarily defined in src/acp/control-plane/manager.core.ts, provides a structured way to orchestrate agent activities. The ACP also manages persistent session bindings, linking specific conversations to agent sessions, which helps maintain context across interactions, as detailed in src/acp/persistent-bindings.lifecycle.ts.

All significant events during an ACP session, such as user prompts and state updates, are recorded in an event ledger. This ledger provides a chronological log of actions, enabling replay and audit capabilities for agent interactions. Both in-memory and file-based persistence options are supported, with configurable storage limits and file locking mechanisms, as implemented in src/acp/event-ledger.ts. Content processing utilities in src/acp/event-mapper.ts are used to extract meaningful data from these events, such as text and attachments from prompts, and to normalize tool call locations.

Policy enforcement is integral to the ACP system, ensuring that agent operations adhere to predefined security and operational guidelines. Policies determine whether ACP is enabled, if agent dispatch is allowed, and what permissions individual agents have. This includes checks for allowed agents and configuration-driven restrictions. Violations trigger specific errors with clear resolution suggestions, as outlined in src/acp/policy.ts. Furthermore, the system incorporates permission relay mechanisms to translate Gateway execution approval events into ACP permission requests and vice versa, bridging the gap between high-level policies and low-level agent actions, evident in src/acp/permission-relay.ts.

The ACP runtime environment provides the secure execution context for agent processes. It includes a registry for managing different ACP runtime backend implementations and robust error handling mechanisms that format and suggest next steps for runtime issues. The runtime also handles session identity and metadata, ensuring that each agent process operates within its defined boundaries. Availability checks for runtime spawning and adherence to a strict adapter contract for implementations ensure reliability and security, primarily managed within the src/acp/runtime directory.
