Security Considerations and Policies
link

The OpenClaw project outlines its security policy and posture in SECURITY.md, guiding users on vulnerability reporting and informing maintainers about the project's trust model. Vulnerabilities should be reported privately, ideally through GitHub Security Advisories for core components, to prevent public disclosure of unpatched issues. Reports require specific details, including the affected component, reproduction steps, and demonstrated impact, to be triaged effectively. Issues frequently deemed out of scope include prompt injection without a specific policy, the misuse of intentional local features by trusted operators, and scanner-only reports not tied to OpenClaw's documented trust boundaries.

OpenClaw operates under an "Operator Trust Model," meaning it is designed as a local-first agent infrastructure for trusted operators. Authenticated callers to the Gateway are treated as trusted. This implies that features like HTTP compatibility endpoints and x-openclaw-scopes headers function within this trusted context. Plugins and extensions are considered part of OpenClaw's trusted computing base and operate with the same privileges as the OpenClaw process itself. Therefore, security reports involving plugins must demonstrate a boundary bypass rather than just malicious behavior from an installed plugin.

Deployment assumptions reinforce this model, expecting the host running OpenClaw to be within a trusted administrative boundary, and advising against sharing a single Gateway among mutually untrusted individuals. The system primarily functions on a "One-User Trust Model," where session identifiers serve as routing controls, not authorization boundaries, recommending isolation for mixed-trust users. Agents and models are not considered trusted principals; the system assumes prompt and content injection can manipulate their behavior. Security boundaries are instead defined by host and configuration trust, authentication, tool policies, sandboxing, and execution approvals.

OpenClaw distinguishes between the Gateway (control plane) and Nodes (execution extensions), both operating within the same operator trust boundary. Execution approvals serve as operator guardrails rather than multi-tenant authorization boundaries. Trusted local operator state, such as MEMORY.md and memory/*.md, is considered a trusted boundary, and memory_search over these files is expected behavior.

For secure deployment, OpenClaw provides operational guidance, including hardening recommendations for tool filesystem access, sub-agent delegation, and web interface safety. It suggests keeping the Gateway loopback-only (gateway.bind="loopback") to avoid public exposure. Minimum Node.js versions are specified due to security patches. When running in Docker, guidelines include using a non-root user, --read-only configurations, and dropping capabilities (--cap-drop=ALL).

Internal security scanning processes leverage various tools for continuous security and release validation. These include secret detection via detect-private-key, static analysis with CodeQL and OpenGrep, and end-to-end and live validation tests. OpenClaw also has a structured incident response process, covering detection, triage, severity assessment, and communication protocols for security vulnerabilities. Furthermore, OpenClaw defines processes for Threat Model Contributions and Analysis and utilizes Formal Verification of Security Policies using TLA+/TLC models to machine-check security claims across critical system domains. Network traffic can be routed through an operator-managed forward proxy to enhance security, with considerations for HTTP/WebSocket proxying, TLS, and mitigating attacks like SSRF and DNS rebinding using tools like Proxyline.

The OpenClaw platform is built upon a set of fundamental concepts that govern its architecture and operational mechanics. These concepts span agent lifecycle, data management, communication protocols, and quality assurance, providing a comprehensive framework for intelligent agent systems.

Central to OpenClaw is the concept of the "agentic loop," which defines the complete lifecycle of an agent's execution, from receiving input to generating a reply. This loop encompasses stages such as intake, context assembly, interaction with AI models, execution of tools, and persisting session state. OpenClaw implements this through core runtimes that manage execution flow and concurrency, ensuring that agent runs are serialized per session to maintain history consistency and prevent race conditions. Agents leverage various entry points, both via remote procedure calls (RPC) and command-line interfaces (CLI), and their execution involves a meticulous process of resolving models, loading skills, and subscribing to event streams for real-time feedback. Further details on this process can be found in Agent Lifecycle and Runtime Mechanisms.

OpenClaw's design includes sophisticated mechanisms for managing conversational context and memory. "Context" refers to all data provided to an AI model, constrained by its token limits, and includes the system prompt, conversation history, tool calls, and results. A pluggable context engine orchestrates the ingestion, assembly, and compaction of this context, ensuring that models receive relevant information efficiently. Compaction is a key strategy for managing long conversation histories, condensing them to fit within model context windows, either automatically or manually. Beyond immediate context, OpenClaw features a comprehensive memory system, utilizing Markdown files (MEMORY.md, memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md, DREAMS.md) to manage long-term facts, daily notes, and consolidated knowledge. This system supports various memory backends, including a built-in SQLite-based engine that combines keyword and vector search capabilities, as well as advanced engines like QMD and Honcho for enhanced search, cross-session memory, and user modeling. Commitments further extend memory by capturing inferred, short-lived follow-ups, while the dreaming system facilitates background memory consolidation. For more information, refer to Context and Memory Management Architecture.

Inter-component communication in OpenClaw relies on a WebSocket gateway that serves as the central hub for interactions between the Gateway daemon, client applications (CLI, mobile, web), and nodes (mobile, headless devices). This gateway utilizes a defined wire protocol with JSON payloads, supports robust authentication, and incorporates idempotency for side-effecting methods to ensure reliable message processing. A crucial architectural pattern is the "delegate architecture," which enables agents to operate with their own identity on behalf of an organization, complete with defined capability tiers and isolation mechanisms for security. The details of these communication and delegation patterns are outlined in Inter-component Communication and Delegation.

For presenting information to users across different communication channels, OpenClaw employs a structured approach to outbound Markdown formatting. This involves a three-step pipeline: parsing Markdown into an Intermediate Representation (IR), chunking the IR to preserve formatting integrity, and then rendering it specifically for each channel (e.g., Slack's mrkdwn, Telegram's HTML). This ensures consistent and accurate display regardless of the destination platform. Additionally, OpenClaw supports "channel docking," a feature that allows redirecting a session's replies between linked chat channels, enhancing user experience by centralizing conversations. These aspects are explored further in Outbound Formatting and Channel Integration.

Quality assurance for OpenClaw's language models and agents is managed through "Mantis," an end-to-end visual verification system. Mantis is designed to reproduce bugs within live transport environments, capture relevant artifacts, and provide deterministic oracles for testing. It integrates with various components to perform automated testing, including desktop browser smoke tests, Discord bot tests, and visual task execution with AI analysis, ensuring the reliability and correctness of agent interactions. For more details, see End-to-End Visual Verification with Mantis.

Agent Lifecycle and Runtime Mechanisms
link
zoom_in

OpenClaw employs a single embedded agent runtime per Gateway, managing its own workspace, bootstrap files, and session store. This runtime executes a prepared model loop, handling prompt reception, driving model output, and making native tool calls.

The core agent lifecycle, known as the agentic loop, processes an agent's turn from intake to persistence. This loop ensures serialized execution per session, emitting lifecycle and stream events to maintain session state consistency. Entry points for initiating agent runs include the agent and agent.wait Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs) via the Gateway, and the agent command in the CLI. The agent RPC validates parameters, resolves and persists session metadata, and immediately returns a runId. The agentCommand orchestrates the run, resolving models, loading skills, and calling the core runtime, runEmbeddedPiAgent. This runtime serializes runs using per-session and global queues, builds the pi session, and subscribes to events for streaming deltas. The subscribeEmbeddedPiSession component bridges events from the core agent to the OpenClaw agent stream, mapping tool events, assistant deltas, and lifecycle events. The agent.wait RPC uses waitForAgentRun to await the completion or error of a specific runId.

To ensure system stability and data integrity, runs are serialized per session key and can optionally be serialized globally. This prevents conflicts during tool and session operations and maintains consistency of session history. Messaging channels can support various queue modes, such as steer, followup, collect, and interrupt, which control how messages are processed during an active run. Session transcripts are stored as JSONL files, and session IDs remain stable across interactions.

Before an agent run, the system prepares the session and workspace. The agent's working directory is resolved and created, potentially in a sandboxed environment if agents.defaults.sandbox is enabled. User-editable files, including AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, TOOLS.md, BOOTSTRAP.md, IDENTITY.md, and USER.md, are injected into the system prompt's project context during a new session's initial turn. These files define the agent's behavior, persona, and initial instructions. Skills are loaded hierarchically from various directories, allowing for customization and overrides. Core tools, such as read, exec, edit, write, and system tools, are always available subject to policy.

OpenClaw offers two main hook systems for extending and modifying agent behavior. Extensions and Plugins System provides more detail on the plugin architecture. Internal hooks, defined as event-driven scripts, respond to commands and lifecycle events, such as agent:bootstrap for modifying bootstrap files. Plugin hooks offer additional extension points within the agent and tool lifecycle, allowing interception of model resolution, prompt building, agent replies, tool calls, and session events.

During execution, assistant deltas are streamed as assistant events, and partial replies can be emitted. Final payloads are assembled from assistant text, inline tool summaries, and assistant error messages, with mechanisms to filter out redundant or suppressed content. Auto-compaction optimizes embedded agent sessions by managing message history, emitting compaction stream events, and triggering retries to reset in-memory buffers. Context and Memory Management Architecture covers these mechanisms in more detail.

Agent runtimes are distinct from providers, models, and channels. A "harness" provides the implementation for an agent runtime. OpenClaw supports different runtime families: embedded harnesses like pi and codex that run within OpenClaw's agent loop, and CLI backends such as claude-cli that execute local CLI processes. The system determines the appropriate runtime based on a hierarchy of policies, starting from model-scoped policies and falling back to provider-scoped configurations. If no specific runtime is claimed, the pi runtime is used as a compatibility layer. The document docs/concepts/agent-runtimes.md provides a comprehensive overview of the different "Codex" surfaces, including the native Codex app-server runtime, its OAuth profiles, the ACP adapter, and chat-control commands, clarifying how they are configured and interact within the OpenClaw ecosystem.

Context and Memory Management Architecture
link
zoom_in

OpenClaw manages how information is supplied to and retained by AI models through a sophisticated context and memory system. The "context" refers to all data—rules, tools, conversation history, and attachments—sent to a model for a given run, constrained by its token limit. This differs from "memory," which represents information durably stored outside the immediate model context.
